questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a heavy nucleus gains on splitting
questions.learningObjective: Explain why splitting a heavy nucleus releases energy
questions.stem: A data table lists 7.6 MeV per nucleon for uranium-235 and 7.9 MeV per nucleon for lead-208. When a uranium-235 nucleus splits, what does the system gain?

options.text: Energy, because the fragments have a higher total binding energy than the parent
Mass, because the fragments together weigh more than the original uranium nucleus
options.misconception: treats missing mass as mass gained, not energy

options.text: Protons, because the fragments have a much higher neutron to proton ratio
options.misconception: thinks fission turns protons into neutrons in fragments

options.text: Charge, because the electron cloud is pushed outward as the nucleus divides
options.misconception: believes fission pushes electrons out of the nucleus

questions.explanation: Fission raises the total binding energy of the fragments, and that increase is released as energy. The fragments weigh slightly less than the parent, so the missing mass is energy.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity is larger for the fragments.

questions.topic: Why the binding curve peaks near iron

questions.stem: A binding curve table gives 7.6 MeV per nucleon for uranium-238 and 8.8 MeV per nucleon for iron-56. What does this pair of values show?

options.text: Fusing light nuclei up to iron releases energy, beyond iron it would cost energy
Iron-56 releases energy when fused, while uranium-238 absorbs energy when fused
options.misconception: assumes binding energy per nucleon never changes

options.text: Both nuclei release the same energy per nucleon when they fuse into heavier ones
options.misconception: ignores the difference between the listed binding energies

options.text: Uranium-238 is closer to the peak of the binding curve than iron-56 actually is
options.misconception: misreads which nucleus sits nearer the peak of the curve

questions.explanation: Iron-56 sits near the peak of the binding curve, so fusion up to that point releases energy. Fusing uranium-238 into something heavier lowers binding energy per nucleon, which costs energy instead.
questions.hint: Compare each nucleus with the peak of the curve.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a mass defect is
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a mass defect represents physically
questions.stem: A table gives 235.2872 u for the free nucleons of one uranium-235 nucleus and 235.0439 u for the assembled nucleus. Explain what the 0.2433 u difference represents and where it goes.

answer.exemplar: The 0.2433 u difference is the mass defect: the assembled nucleus is lighter than the sum of its separate protons and neutrons because binding energy holds them together. That missing mass has been converted into binding energy inside the nucleus, and it reappears as energy when the nucleus is broken up or rearranged.

questions.explanation: The gap between the summed free nucleon masses and the assembled nucleus is the mass defect, matching the binding energy. Breaking the nucleus returns that mass as energy.
questions.hint: Think of the gap as the energy stored by binding.

questions.stem: A reference table shows that one elastic collision with a hydrogen nucleus reduces a neutron energy by a factor of ten. How many collisions are needed to bring a 1.00 MeV neutron down to 0.001 MeV?

questions.learningObjective: Explain the fate of the missing mass in a fission
questions.stem: A table shows a uranium-235 nucleus of mass 235.0439 u and the same nucleus after splitting into two fragments of total mass 234.8000 u. Explain the source of the 0.2439 u of missing mass.

answer.exemplar: The missing 0.2439 u is the mass defect, converted into energy by the strong nuclear force that binds the nucleons together. When the nucleus splits, the fragments are less tightly bound, so that binding energy is released, most of it as kinetic energy of the fission fragments and neutrons.

questions.explanation: The missing mass is the mass equivalent of the binding energy that held the nucleus together. Splitting lowers total binding energy, and the difference appears as kinetic energy.
questions.hint: Mass and energy are two views of one quantity.

options.misconception: calls the assembly critical though the count is falling

questions.stem: A table lists a physical half-life of 6.01 hours for a tracer and a biological half-life of 12.0 hours for the same tracer in tissue. Explain why the tracer disappears faster inside the body than in a sealed vial.

answer.exemplar: In a sealed vial the only loss is radioactive decay, with the 6.01 hour physical half-life. questions.explanation: Physical half-life is set by the nucleus alone, while biological half-life is set by removal from the body. In tissue both act at once, so the tracer vanishes faster than 6.01 hours suggests.
